```{.quiz-yaml}
id: 08_hypothesis_testing_choose_in_advance
title: >
  Choose Before Looking
questions:
  - id: wrong_direction
    type: multiple-choice
    prompt: >
      Before collecting any data, a researcher predicts that a treatment will
      *reduce* scores, and specifies a lower-tailed test with $\alpha = .05$.
      The study produces $z = +2.40$. What should they conclude?
    options:
      - text: >
          Fail to reject the null hypothesis, because the result is not in the
          lower-tailed critical region
        correct: true
      - text: >
          Reject the null hypothesis, because $z = 2.40$ is beyond 1.96
      - text: >
          Switch to a two-tailed test, since the result turned out to be in the
          other direction
      - text: >
          Switch to an upper-tailed test and reject the null hypothesis
    explanation: >
      With all of $\alpha$ in the lower tail, the only critical region lies
      below about $-1.64$, so $z = +2.40$ is not in it; its lower-tailed $p$ is
      about .99. Switching to a two-tailed or upper-tailed test after seeing
      the result would mean choosing the decision rule to fit the data. The
      unexpected increase might be worth following up, but as an exploratory
      finding to test with new data.

  - id: changing_alpha_after_results
    type: multiple-choice
    prompt: >
      A researcher planned to use $\alpha = .01$ and obtained $p = .032$. The
      pattern looks interesting, so after seeing the result they switch to
      $\alpha = .05$ and call it a confirmed finding. What would be more
      appropriate?
    options:
      - text: >
          Report that the result did not meet the planned criterion, treat the
          pattern as exploratory, and test it with new data
        correct: true
      - text: >
          Keep $\alpha = .05$, because .05 is the most common convention
      - text: >
          Change to a one-tailed test as well, to make the evidence stronger
      - text: >
          Round $p$ down to .01 so that it matches the original criterion
    explanation: >
      Under the planned rule, $.032 > .01$, so the result is not statistically
      significant. The pattern might still be worth exploring, but changing the
      rule after seeing the data draws the target around the result rather than
      testing the result against a target fixed in advance.
```
